1.d4 d5 2.c4.name: Queen's Gambit
1.d4 d5 2.c4.background: One of the oldest known openings: it is mentioned in the Göttingen manuscript of 1490 and was analysed by Gioachino Greco in the 17th century. It did not become common until the 1873 Vienna tournament, and it was played in all but two of the 34 games of the 1927 World Championship match between Capablanca and Alekhine.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 e6.strategy: Supports d5 with the e-pawn and builds a solid centre that Black can hold for a long time. White keeps the tension on d5 and usually has a little more space. The cost is the c8-bishop, shut in behind e6, which needs a freeing pawn break or a fianchetto before it plays a part.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 c6.strategy: Defends d5 with the c-pawn and keeps the c8-bishop's diagonal open, so the bishop is not buried behind the pawn chain. If Black later takes on c4, the c6-pawn supports ...b5 to hold the pawn or to gain time against the capturing piece. The drawbacks are that c6 develops no piece and takes that square from the b8-knight, and that the freeing break ...c5 costs a tempo.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 dxc4.strategy: Takes the pawn and gives up the centre in return for free piece play. Black usually lets White regain the pawn and spends the time striking at White's centre, because holding the pawn tends to be unprofitable. White's aim is to use the extra space in the centre to build an attack.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 Nc6.strategy: Develops with quick pressure on d4, but the knight blocks the c-pawn and Black no longer holds d5 with a pawn. Black gets active pieces in return and must be willing to trade a bishop for a knight. It is playable and a useful surprise, but its theory is less developed than that of the main defences.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 Bf5.name: Baltic Defence
1.d4 d5 2.c4 Bf5.background: Also known as the Grau Defence and the Sahovic Defence. Grandmasters including Paul Keres and Alexei Shirov have used it, but it has not found widespread acceptance among chess masters.
1.d4 d5 2.c4 Bf5.strategy: Develops the bishop before ...e6 can shut it in, but leaves b7 undefended, so 3.Qb3 hits it at once, and after an exchange on d5 White gains time against Black's queen and bishop. It is an offbeat but playable way to solve the problem of the c8-bishop.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 e5.name: Albin Countergambit
1.d4 d5 2.c4 e5.background: Takes its name from Adolf Albin, who played it against Emanuel Lasker in New York in 1893, although Cavallotti had played it against Salvioli at the Milan tournament of 1881. Alexander Morozevich made some successful use of it in the 2000s.
1.d4 d5 2.c4 e5.strategy: Sacrifices a pawn for a wedge on d4 and some attacking chances, developing quickly and often castling queenside. White usually returns the pawn at a good moment to gain a positional edge. The pawn on d4 is stronger than it looks, so careless play by White is punished.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 c5.strategy: Mirrors White's move and challenges d4 at once. After cxd5 Black should not retake with the queen, since White then develops with a gain of time. Theory holds that White keeps an edge and that Black plays at best for a draw.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 Nf6.strategy: Develops the knight and is sound, since 3.cxd5 Nxd5 loses no material, but 4.e4 drives the knight away with a gain of time and gives White a broad pawn centre. Supporting d5 with a pawn first avoids this.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 Na6.strategy: Aims at b4 from the rim but does nothing in the centre and leaves d5 to the queen alone. After 3.cxd5 Qxd5 4.Nc3 the queen is driven back, and White leads in development.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 Be6.strategy: Guards d5 a second time, but the bishop blocks the e-pawn and leaves b7 undefended. After 3.cxd5 Bxd5 4.Nc3 it comes under attack again, and White develops with a gain of time.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 Bg4.strategy: Gets the bishop out early, but on g4 it hits only the well-defended e2-pawn and leaves b7 undefended. 3.cxd5 Qxd5 4.Nc3 gains time against the queen, and a pawn move later chases the bishop.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 Qd7.strategy: Keeps d5 guarded but puts the queen on d7, where it blocks the c8-bishop and takes d7 from the b8-knight. After 3.cxd5 Qxd5 4.Nc3 the queen has to move again, and White is ahead in development.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 Qd6.strategy: Brings the queen out early to hold d5, but after 3.cxd5 Qxd5 4.Nc3 it must move again while White develops with tempo.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 Nh6.strategy: Heads for f5 from the rim, but the c1-bishop already eyes h6: 3.Bxh6 gxh6 wrecks Black's kingside pawns, with only the bishop pair in return. The d5 pawn is also left to the queen.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 a6.strategy: Prepares ...b5 for the case of ...dxc4, but spends a tempo on a rook-pawn move and leaves d5 to the queen. After 3.cxd5 Qxd5 4.Nc3 the queen is attacked and must retreat.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 a5.strategy: A wing move that weakens b5 and contributes nothing to the centre or development. White plays 3.cxd5 Qxd5 4.Nc3 and gains a tempo against the queen.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 b6.strategy: Prepares ...Bb7, but there the bishop would face its own d5-pawn, and d5 is left to the queen alone. 3.cxd5 Qxd5 4.Nc3 drives the queen off with a gain of time.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 f6.strategy: Takes f6 from the knight and weakens e6 and the e8-h5 diagonal, while neither supporting d5 nor developing a piece. White answers 3.cxd5 Qxd5 4.Nc3 and gains a tempo.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 f5.strategy: Stakes out e4 with a kingside pawn, but leaves d5 to the queen and weakens e6 and the e8-h5 diagonal. 3.cxd5 Qxd5 4.Nc3 gains time against the queen.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 g6.strategy: Prepares to fianchetto the king's bishop, a sound idea, but leaves d5 to the queen alone. 3.cxd5 Qxd5 4.Nc3 chases the queen away with a gain of time, and White keeps the bigger centre.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 h6.strategy: Takes g5 from the c1-bishop, but it is a slow rim-pawn move that does nothing for d5 or development. After 3.cxd5 Qxd5 4.Nc3 White hits the queen with tempo.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 h5.strategy: Spends a tempo on the rim and loosens g5 and g6, with no connection to d5 or to development. White answers 3.cxd5 Qxd5 4.Nc3 and develops with a gain of time.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 Nd7.strategy: Blocks the queen's defence of d5, so 3.cxd5 wins a pawn: after 3...Ngf6 4.Nc3 and e4 White keeps it. The knight on d7 also shuts in the c8-bishop.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 Bd7.strategy: Blocks the queen's defence of d5, so 3.cxd5 wins a pawn that no black piece can retake at once. The bishop on d7 is passive and takes d7 from the b8-knight.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 Bh3.strategy: Gives away the bishop for nothing: 3.gxh3 takes it, and no black piece can recapture on h3, so Black has no compensation at all.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 Kd7.strategy: Gives up castling and blocks the queen's defence of d5, so 3.cxd5 wins a pawn that cannot be retaken at once. The king is left in the middle with nothing in return.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 b5.name: Queen's Gambit Declined: Zilbermints Gambit
1.d4 d5 2.c4 b5.strategy: Gambits the b-pawn to deflect White's c-pawn: 3.cxb5 takes it, since nothing can recapture, and Black has no lead in development to make up for it. The queenside is loosened for good, and White keeps the extra pawn and the better centre.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 g5.strategy: Leaves the g-pawn en prise: 3.Bxg5 takes it along the open c1-h6 diagonal, and nothing of Black's can retake, since the queen's diagonal is blocked by e7. The kingside is loosened for good with no development in return.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 Bf5 3.Qb3.name: Queen's Gambit Declined: Baltic Defence, Queen Attack
1.d4 d5 2.c4 Bf5 3.Qb3.strategy: Hits b7, which nothing guards now that the bishop has left c8, while the c4 pawn already bears on d5. Black has only a few good answers, such as a counter-sacrifice in the centre, so the sortie costs something, but the edge is small.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 Bf5 3.cxd5.strategy: Takes the pawn, which Black soon wins back, either with a knight or by first trading the bishop for the b1 knight and recapturing with the queen. White keeps the d4 pawn and a modest, lasting edge with little risk.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 Bf5 3.Nc3.strategy: Develops and adds a second attacker to d5, so Black must defend the pawn at once, and prepares e4 against the f5 bishop. Sound and healthy, but Black can simply support d5 with ...e6, which keeps the bishop outside the pawn chain, and White's edge is small.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 Bf5 3.cxd5 Bxb1.strategy: Takes the knight while the diagonal is open. Recapturing the pawn with the queen instead lets White gain time by developing with tempo against queen and bishop; the trade costs Black the bishop pair but keeps the position healthy, and the d5 pawn is won back later.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 Bf5 3.cxd5 Qxd5.strategy: Takes the pawn at once with the queen, but the queen is then driven around with tempo: White develops with a threat against it and next attacks the bishop on f5 as well. Black loses time while White builds a broad centre.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 Bf5 3.cxd5 Nf6.strategy: Brings a piece out and prepares to retake on d5 with the knight, keeping the queen at home. Black is a pawn down for the moment and has to win it back at once, with the bishop on f5 still exposed to White's central pawn advance.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 Bf5 3.cxd5 Bxb1 4.Qa4+.strategy: Checks before recapturing, so the bishop on b1 has no time to escape and the rook takes it next. Sound, but the check lets Black block with ...c6, which attacks d5 at once and builds a solid centre, so White gains less than the simple recapture.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 Bf5 3.cxd5 Bxb1 4.Rxb1.strategy: Recaptures the bishop at once. Black retakes d5 with the queen, which centralises it and eyes the loose a2 pawn, but White has the bishop pair and the space of the d4 pawn, and keeps a small, lasting edge.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 Bf5 3.cxd5 Bxb1 4.Nf3.strategy: Develops but lets the bishop on b1 out: it simply retreats along the diagonal, and Black keeps the knight it won for a single pawn. White has thrown away the whole point of the capture on d5.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 Bf5 3.cxd5 Bxb1 4.Qa4+ c6.strategy: Blocks the check with a pawn that attacks d5, the pawn White captured. The b1 bishop falls to the rook next, in return for the knight it took, so Black's task is to win the pawn back and reach a solid game.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 Bf5 3.cxd5 Bxb1 4.Qa4+ Qd7.strategy: Blocks the check with the queen and offers its exchange. After the swap Black retakes with a developing knight, wins the d5 pawn back once the rook has taken the bishop, and reaches a simple, level position without weaknesses.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 Bf5 3.cxd5 Bxb1 4.Qa4+ Nd7.strategy: Blocks the check with the other knight, which is then pinned to the king by the queen on a4. After 5.Rxb1 White is a pawn up, and the pinned knight makes it slow for Black to win d5 back, so White keeps the pawn and the initiative for longer.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 Bf5 3.cxd5 Bxb1 4.Qa4+ c6 5.strategy: Greedily takes a second pawn instead of simply collecting the trapped bishop. The extra pawn does not last: Black's recapture hits d4, and the queen swap that follows leaves a level endgame, so White gives up the better way to keep a small plus.

Collects the bishop at once and gives the extra pawn back. The queen on a4 pins the c6 pawn, so only the queen can retake d5. Material is level and White keeps a small, more comfortable edge from the space of the d4 pawn.
Develops while the bishop is still on b1, and so lets it out: it slips away to f5 and Black keeps the knight it won, with White having only a pawn for it. The bishop should be taken at once.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 Bf5 3.cxd5 Bxb1 4.Qa4+ c6 5.name: Queen's Gambit Declined: Baltic Defence, Argentinian Gambit
1.d4 d5 2.c4 Bf5 3.cxd5 Bxb1 4.Qa4+ c6 5.strategy: Recaptures with a developing move that attacks d4, which is now attacked twice and held once. Black wins the pawn back once White has taken the bishop, and the queen swap that follows is level. The knight is pinned to the king meanwhile, but only until the queen leaves a4.
Retakes with the b-pawn, which does not touch d4. Once the rook has taken the bishop on b1, Black is a pawn down and is left with an isolated a-pawn, with nothing to compensate.
Walks into the pawn on c6: it takes the knight with check, the queen has to retake, and Black has lost a whole piece for nothing.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 Bf5 3.Nc3 e6.strategy: Defends d5, which the knight and the c-pawn both attack, and frees the f8 bishop. Black's light-squared bishop is already outside the pawn chain, which avoids the usual problem of this opening, at the price of a slightly passive centre against White's extra space.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 Bf5 3.Nc3 Nf6.strategy: Brings the kingside knight out and adds a second defender to d5. The cost is a passive set-up: the f8 bishop stays shut in behind the e-pawn, and White decides how the centre is settled, with Black reacting to a queen sortie or the pawn advance in the centre.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 Bf5 3.Nc3 dxc4.strategy: Wins a pawn that White regains with tempo: a central pawn push attacks the bishop on f5. Black has to retreat it, since taking the pawn loses a piece, and White gets a broad centre and the lead in development.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 Bf5 3.Nc3 e6 4.Nf3.strategy: The natural developing move: the knight guards d4 and e5, so the queen can later go to b3 against b7 without leaving the d4 pawn loose. White develops in order and keeps a slight edge from the extra space.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 Bf5 3.Nc3 e6 4.Qb3.name: Queen's Gambit Declined: Baltic Defence, Queen Attack Deferred
1.d4 d5 2.c4 Bf5 3.Nc3 e6 4.Qb3.strategy: Hits b7 but comes early: with the knight still on g1, the d4 pawn has no defender, so Black develops with tempo by attacking it. Sound, since d4 can still be defended, but White gains less than the sortie suggests, and a grab on d5 can run into a counterstrike against d4.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 Bf5 3.Nc3 e6 4.cxd5.strategy: Releases the tension and leaves Black a pawn on d5 with the bishop outside it, a solid symmetrical set-up. White follows with a queen move that hits d5 and b7 together and keeps a small initiative.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 Bf5 3.Nc3 e6 4.Nf3 c6.name: Queen's Gambit Declined: Baltic Defence, Pseudo-Slav
1.d4 d5 2.c4 Bf5 3.Nc3 e6 4.Nf3 c6.strategy: Supports d5 with a second pawn, so the e6 and c6 pawns make a compact barrier with the bishop outside it. Black is solid, but concedes space: White keeps a slight edge and the more comfortable game.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 Bf5 3.Nc3 e6 4.Nf3 Nc6.name: Queen's Gambit Declined: Baltic Defence, Pseudo-Chigorin
1.d4 d5 2.c4 Bf5 3.Nc3 e6 4.Nf3 Nc6.strategy: Develops with pressure on d4 and keeps the c-pawn free to strike at the centre later. In return d5 rests on the e6 pawn and the queen alone, which asks for care once White starts exchanging on d5.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 Bf5 3.Nc3 e6 4.Nf3 Nf6.strategy: Develops the kingside knight, protects d5 once more and prepares to castle. Black keeps the c-pawn and the queen's knight flexible, but b7 is loose to a queen sortie to b3, so Black must be ready to meet it.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 e5 3.dxe5.strategy: Accepts the gambit at once, the principled reply. White is a pawn up and Black has to justify the sacrifice with fast development and central pressure, while White aims to return the pawn at the right moment for a positional edge.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 e5 3.cxd5.strategy: Takes the d5 pawn and sidesteps the gambit, but ...Qxd5 at once attacks d4 a second time, with the e-pawn and the queen. The queens usually come off with material level, which leads to a quiet position with no lasting edge for either side.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 e5 3.e3.strategy: Defends d4 but lets Black trade it off with ...exd4. After the exchange Black develops easily, with the d5 pawn pressing on c4, and gets the slightly easier game; White's centre is no longer an asset. Sound, but White passes up the extra pawn on offer.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 e5 3.dxe5 d4.strategy: The point of the gambit: the pawn becomes a wedge that cramps White, taking the c3 and e3 squares away from White's pieces. Black gives up a pawn for space and some chances of an attack, and must keep the wedge supported.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 e5 3.dxe5 dxc4.strategy: Wins the pawn back at once, so material is level, but the wedge is never built. White trades queens with check, Black's king must recapture and loses the right to castle, and the pawn on e5 cramps Black's pieces. White keeps a clear edge.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 e5 3.dxe5 Nc6.strategy: Develops and attacks the e5 pawn, but allows cxd5: ...Qxd5 then loses the queen to Qxd5 now that the d-file is open, so Black has to recapture on e5 with the knight. Black ends a clean pawn down and without the d4 wedge.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 e5 3.dxe5 d4 4.Nf3.name: Queen's Gambit Declined: Albin Countergambit, Normal Line
1.d4 d5 2.c4 e5 3.dxe5 d4 4.Nf3.strategy: Develops a piece against the wedge: it attacks d4 and guards the extra pawn on e5. White keeps the pawn without weakening anything and sidesteps the careless pawn pushes that run into trouble, so Black has to justify the gambit by active development.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 e5 3.dxe5 d4 4.e3.strategy: Challenges the wedge too early and walks into the Lasker Trap: after ...Bb4+ Bd2 dxe3, taking the bishop on b4 loses at once. Recapturing on e3 with the f-pawn avoids it, but leaves White's king's side thinner and the game stays level. Sound, but risky and it gains nothing.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 e5 3.dxe5 d4 4.e4.name: Queen's Gambit Declined: Albin Countergambit, Spassky Variation
1.d4 d5 2.c4 e5 3.dxe5 d4 4.e4.strategy: Avoids the Lasker Trap by advancing two squares: Black can capture en passant only at once. The wedge on d4 stays unchallenged and the pawn on e5 has to be defended, but the position is balanced; White gets no more from the extra pawn than Black gets for it.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 e5 3.dxe5 d4 4.e3 Bb4+.strategy: Gives check on the diagonal that White's d-pawn has left open, so White must spend a move on the king. The bishop also sets up the tactic that makes 4.e3 so dangerous: the d4 pawn attacks e3, and Black can capture there with a powerful bishop on b4.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 e5 3.dxe5 d4 4.e3 Nc6.strategy: Defends the wedge with a developing move and keeps the bishop check in reserve. If White takes on d4 the knight can recapture, but Black is still a pawn down and plays for development and open lines without the trap.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 e5 3.dxe5 d4 4.e3 c5.strategy: Backs the wedge with a pawn, but the pawn closes the diagonal to b4 and with it the check and the trap. White develops and builds up pressure on d4, and Black is a pawn down with little to show for it.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 e5 3.dxe5 d4 4.e3 Bb4+ 5.Bd.strategy: The natural way to meet the check: it develops a piece and offers to trade off Black's active bishop. But e3 is still attacked by the wedge, and the bishop on d2 is the piece White must not be tempted to use for a hasty capture on b4.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 e5 3.dxe5 d4 4.e3 Bb4+ 5.Nd.strategy: Blocks with the knight instead of the bishop. It develops a piece, but the knight stays pinned to the king by the bishop on b4 and shuts in the c1 bishop, so White is slow to catch up in development against the pressure on e3.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 e5 3.dxe5 d4 4.e3 Bb4+ 5.Nc.strategy: Loses a piece: the knight steps into the pin and the d4 pawn simply takes it. Recapturing with bxc3 only makes it worse, since ...Bxc3+ is check and hits the rook on a1.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 e5 3.dxe5 d4 4.e3 Bb4+ 5.Bd.name: Queen's Gambit Declined: Albin Countergambit, Lasker Trap
1.d4 d5 2.c4 e5 3.dxe5 d4 4.e3 Bb4+ 5.Bd.background: Named after Emanuel Lasker, although Serafino Dubois noted the trap first. In a consultation game at Moscow in 1899, Lasker, as Black, played into this position against Blumenfeld, Boyarkow and Falk.
1.d4 d5 2.c4 e5 3.dxe5 d4 4.e3 Bb4+ 5.Bd.strategy: Springs the trap. Black ignores the bishop on b4 and takes on e3: if White greedily takes that bishop, ...exf2+ and a promotion to a knight on g1 win decisively. The safe reply is to recapture and accept doubled pawns, which still leaves Black slightly better.

Trades the active bishop for the one White has just developed and so gives up the trap. White recaptures with the queen and keeps the extra pawn with a safe position, while Black has only development to show for it.

Retreats and gives up the wedge for nothing: White takes on d4 and is two pawns up, with the bishop on d2 already developed. Black has lost the trap and has little but quick development to show for the pawns.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 e5 3.dxe5 d4 4.Nf3 Nc6.strategy: The main line. The knight guards the d4 wedge, attacks the e5 pawn and keeps the bishop's diagonal to b4 open. Black recovers the pawn only if White neglects it, so White must watch e5 while finishing development.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 e5 3.dxe5 d4 4.Nf3 c5.name: Queen's Gambit Declined: Albin Countergambit, Tartakower Defence
1.d4 d5 2.c4 e5 3.dxe5 d4 4.Nf3 c5.strategy: Supports the wedge with a pawn, but the same pawn closes the diagonal to b4, so Black no longer has the check that makes a pawn strike at the wedge dangerous. White hits d4 with e3 at once, keeps the extra pawn, and Black gets little for it.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 e5 3.dxe5 d4 4.Nf3 Bb4+.strategy: Checks at once, but nothing comes of it: White blocks with Nbd2, a developing move, and the pin on that knight achieves little. Black is still a pawn down and has spent a move on the bishop instead of developing the knight to defend the wedge.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 e5 3.dxe5 d4 4.Nf3 Nc6 5.g3.name: Queen's Gambit Declined: Albin Countergambit, Fianchetto Variation
1.d4 d5 2.c4 e5 3.dxe5 d4 4.Nf3 Nc6 5.g3.strategy: Prepares to fianchetto the king's bishop to the long diagonal, a sound set-up and White's surest way to keep a small edge. The bishop will pressure c6 and the queenside and shield the king, and the plan leaves the extra pawn in White's hands for now.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 e5 3.dxe5 d4 4.Nf3 Nc6 5.Nb.name: Queen's Gambit Declined: Albin Countergambit, Modern Line
1.d4 d5 2.c4 e5 3.dxe5 d4 4.Nf3 Nc6 5.Nb.strategy: Develops the knight to a square the wedge does not attack, backing up the knight that guards e5 and covering c4. It is a quieter set-up than the fianchetto: it blocks the c1-bishop and gives Black time to gather pieces against e5.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 e5 3.dxe5 d4 4.Nf3 Nc6 5.a3.strategy: Takes b4 away from Black's dark-squared bishop, so ...Bb4+ is no longer available, and prepares to challenge the wedge with e3 without fearing the check. A patient set-up: White keeps the extra pawn and waits for Black to commit.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 e5 3.dxe5 d4 4.Nf3 Nc6 5.g3.name: Queen's Gambit Declined: Albin Countergambit, Fianchetto Variation, Be6 Line
1.d4 d5 2.c4 e5 3.dxe5 d4 4.Nf3 Nc6 5.g3.strategy: Develops with a hit on c4, but White guards the pawn with a developing move and completes the fianchetto, so the bishop gains nothing. The pawn on e5 stays in White's hands, and Black has not yet added a second attacker against it.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 e5 3.dxe5 d4 4.Nf3 Nc6 5.g3.name: Queen's Gambit Declined: Albin Countergambit, Fianchetto Variation, Bg4 Line
1.d4 d5 2.c4 e5 3.dxe5 d4 4.Nf3 Nc6 5.g3.strategy: Eyes the knight that guards e5, but nothing is forced: White completes the fianchetto and development, and even the exchange on f3 leaves White clearly better. A knight to e7, preparing a second attacker on e5, goes after the pawn more accurately.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 e5 3.dxe5 d4 4.Nf3 Nc6 5.g3.name: Queen's Gambit Declined: Albin Countergambit, Fianchetto Variation, Bf5 Line
1.d4 d5 2.c4 e5 3.dxe5 d4 4.Nf3 Nc6 5.g3.strategy: Puts the bishop outside the pawn chain on the active diagonal, but it neither attacks e5 nor supports the wedge. White completes the fianchetto and development at leisure, and Black is simply a pawn down.

Heads for g6 to attack e5 a second time before White can consolidate it. Black's other developing moves let White finish the fianchetto in peace; this is the only one that keeps the position level. The knight on c6 keeps the wedge on d4 defended.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 e5 3.dxe5 d4 4.Nf3 Nc6 5.Nb.name: Queen's Gambit Declined: Albin Countergambit, Balogh Variation
1.d4 d5 2.c4 e5 3.dxe5 d4 4.Nf3 Nc6 5.Nb.strategy: Adds a second attacker to e5, but regaining the pawn costs the wedge: after the trades on e5 the other knight comes to f3, hits the queen and d4 falls. The queen also blocks the king's bishop, so Black ends a pawn down and undeveloped.

Eyes the knight that guards e5, but nothing is forced: White continues with the fianchetto and keeps the extra pawn. A bishop on g4 does not help to win the pawn back, and Black has not developed the knight that would attack e5 again.

1.d4 d5 2.c4 e5 3.dxe5 d4 4.Nf3 Nc6 5.Nb.name: Queen's Gambit Declined: Albin Countergambit, Janowski Variation
1.d4 d5 2.c4 e5 3.dxe5 d4 4.Nf3 Nc6 5.Nb.strategy: Attacks e5 with a pawn, but White takes on f6 and the knight recaptures, so the pawn Black meant to win back is simply traded off. Black stays a pawn down, and with the f-pawn gone the king's side is looser.

Heads for g6 to attack e5 a second time, the same idea as against the fianchetto. White cannot keep both the extra pawn and the central grip: either e5 falls or the wedge is traded for it, and the game is level. The knight on c6 keeps d4 defended.

Asks the bishop to decide at once, and the trade on f3 gives White the bishop pair. But the knight that recaptures leaves d2, so ...Bb4+ comes with tempo and Black has good chances to win e5 back; the fianchetto holds the pawn more securely.

Prepares the fianchetto of the king's bishop, White's most reliable plan against the gambit. The bishop on g2 will aim down the long diagonal at Black's queenside while the king castles into safety, and Black usually answers by castling queenside.

Takes b4 from Black's dark-squared bishop, so it cannot pin the knight on d2 to the king. A cautious waiting move: it removes one source of counterplay but does nothing about the bishop on g4, which can take on f3 whenever Black likes.

Cashes in the bishop before it is chased. The recapture brings the knight back to f3, where it still guards e5 and attacks the wedge, but White has the bishop pair and Black must prove the pawn is worth it.

Declines the exchange and keeps the bishop, but on h5 it is out of play and can be driven back by a kingside pawn push. White spends the time consolidating the extra pawn, and Black has to weaken the king's side to keep the bishop in play.
Avoids the exchange on f3 and keeps the bishop pair. The cost is time: the bishop has moved twice while White finishes development, and Black must still prove that the pawn is worth it.
